subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How many lattice points are there in one unit cell of a face centred cubic lattice? (face centred tetragonal lattice)

verification.note: Unit 1 (Solid State) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.62-64, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK GAP: the printed question carries the parenthesis "(face centered tetragonal lattice)" but the printed answer never mentions the tetragonal case at all (book p.62, VSAQ 5). It is answered here: a face centred tetragonal cell has the same 8 corners and 6 face centres, so the count is also 14. SPELLING: the book prints "centered"; "centred" is used here to match the rest of the bank. The distinction between the 14 lattice POINTS and the 4 effective particles is the book's own bracketed line and is kept, because a student who reports 4 to a question asking for lattice points is answering a different question.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Where the points lie
lines: In a face centred arrangement there are
8 lattice points at the corners of the cube
and 6 lattice points at the face centres.
A face centred tetragonal cell has the same
steps.why: The count comes from the positions, so the positions have to be named first. A cube has 8 corners and 6 faces, and the face centred pattern puts one lattice point on each of them. Stretching the cube into a tetragonal cell changes the edge lengths but not the number of corners or faces, so the same count applies.
common_mistakes: Counting 4 face centres instead of 6. A cube has six faces, not four.
Adding a body centre. A face centred cell has no lattice point at the centre of the body.
steps.memory_tip: A cube has 8 corners and 6 faces. Face centred means one point on each of those 14 places.
steps.margin_note: Name the two sets of positions before the arithmetic. The positions carry the first mark on their own.

steps.label: The count
lines: Number of particles per unit cell:
steps.why: The question asks for lattice points, so the answer is the plain count 14. The second line answers the different question a student often confuses with it: each corner point is shared by 8 cells and each face centre by 2, so only 4 particles belong to one cell.
common_mistakes: Writing 4 as the number of lattice points. 4 is the number of particles that belong to the cell; the number of lattice points is 14.
Dividing the face centre by 4 instead of 2. A face is shared between two cells only.
steps.memory_tip: Corner is shared by 8 cells, face by 2. 8 × ⅛ = 1 and 6 × ½ = 3, so 4 in all.
steps.margin_note: Box the 14 as the answer to the question asked, then add the 4 as the particle count with its working.

insider_note: The question says lattice points, so 14 is the answer being marked. Write the 4 particles as a second line with its working; a student who writes only 4 has answered a different question.
